name: Brownish Red
lede: Brownish red is the plain description of a red darkened toward brown, and it is also a formal colour in Werner's mineral nomenclature, where it was number 99 and was matched to a bird's throat and a piece of flint.

sections.title: A description more than a name
sections.body:
Brownish red is a plain description of a colour between [[red]] and [[brown]], and English has collected a crowd of older words that dictionaries gloss with it [11]. Paterson's dictionary defines [[auburn]] as a brownish red or golden brown, used of hair, and notes that the word comes from the Latin for white, *albus*, and shifted meaning in the sixteenth century [11]. It also lists *rufous*, which it defines as brownish red, and *brique*, a lighter brownish red that Paterson finds only in the OED and French dictionaries [11].

Trade names pile up the same way. [[indian-red]] is a dark brownish red made from iron oxide, [[light-red]] is a brownish red made by calcining yellow ochre, and Turkey red, the alizarin dye from [[madder]], is sometimes described as a brownish red [11]. The chrysanthemum gave its name to a pair of colours, vivid yellow and brownish red [11].

Because the phrase is a description, it travels easily between fields. A geologist can use it for flint, a dyer for a cloth and a paint-maker for an earth. This article follows it through Werner's mineral colours, Roman and Renaissance dyeing, the paint-box and the archive [11].

sections.title: Werner's number 99
sections.body:
The name is a formal term in the oldest widely used colour-naming system for natural history. In 1774 the German geologist Abraham Gottlob Werner devised a nomenclature of 54 colours to help identify minerals, and he kept revising it for about forty years [2]. In 1814 the Scottish artist Patrick Syme expanded it with painted swatches and added examples from animals, plants and minerals, and the second edition followed in 1821 [2][3]. Charles Darwin probably met the nomenclature as a student in Edinburgh, and used it on the voyage of HMS *Beagle* [2].

Syme's chart of reds in the 1821 edition kept four of Werner's originals, including number 99, Brownish Red [3]. His recipe for it is a mixture: [[chocolate-red]] blended with [[hyacinth-red]] and a little chestnut brown [1]. His examples were the mark on the throat of the red-throated diver, a bird now called the red-throated loon, and the mineral iron flint, a kind of quartz [1]. Chocolate red, the colour next to it, was not Werner's at all but one of the reds Syme added himself in 1814 [3].

The modern edition of Syme's book adds more examples to the entry: the petals of the Carolina allspice, and an iron ore [1]. Its editors warn that the swatches in the old book have become more muted with age, so the colour seen in a surviving copy is a faded one [2]. Our library carries Werner's number 99 among its sources for the name, dated 1821 [15].

sections.title: Dyers, saints and the ugliest colour
sections.body:
Brownish reds were a trade category long before they were a colour name. Pastoureau reports that the guild of dyers in late Republican Rome distinguished six categories of artisan for red and its neighbouring tones [4]. One of them was the *spadicarii*, who made dark and brownish reds from various wood-based dyes [4]. A second Roman listing, from the dyers' regulations, again names five groups for red tones, and again includes the spadicarii for dark, brownish reds from wood [5].

The colour had a harder time later. In the sixteenth century, writers of moral colour codes distrusted shades of red that tended toward yellow or brown, and linked them with the fires of hell, original sin and vices such as pride, falsehood and lust [6]. *Roux* (russet) was the worst of red and yellow in one shade, and *tanné*, a kind of brownish red or dark russet, was called by many texts of the 1500s the ugliest of all the colours [6]. The same period's turn against showy red, driven by sumptuary laws and the Reformation, did not help [6].

The colour came back through politics. In the early summer of 1789, according to Pastoureau, the pairing of red with a dark brownish shade stood for the city of Paris and its officials far more often than the later red-and-blue pairing did [7]. The blue-white-red cockade did not exist until mid-July 1789 [7].

sections.title: Earths, rust and residue
sections.body:
Most of the brownish reds in a painter's box are iron. Gurney notes that the brownish reds and oranges of iron oxides were simply dug from open pits, which is why red, black and yellow turn up in every early art [10]. Ball describes burnt [[sienna]] as taking on a warm brownish-red shade when the yellow earth is roasted [9], and light red and its cousin [[english-red]] were brownish reds made by burning yellow ochre in the eighteenth century [12].

The laboratory made more. Colcothar, in the Oxford English Dictionary's definition, is the brownish red peroxide of iron left in the retort after sulphuric acid is distilled from iron sulphate, and a French author of 1785 appears to treat it as the same as caput mortuum [12]. Prussian brown was made by charring Prussian blue: Bouvier, in 1827, warned that too intense a blue gave a heavy, opaque brownish red, and a too-aluminous one a feeble, yellowish tint [12].

Some brownish reds come from living things. The resin of the gamboge tree is brownish red in its hardened state and turns bright yellow once ground [12]. Dragon's blood, a resin carried up the Red Sea from Yemen, is a brownish-red powder, and Finlay notes it gained its name through a pile of tales about saints, princes and beasts that the true source, a tree sap, hardly bears out [13]. The oxidised form of haemoglobin is also a brownish-red powder, and it was once used to tint paint [12].

sections.title: On the walls
sections.body:
Brownish red is the colour of ordinary painted surfaces as much as of fine art. Ball tells how the architect Owen Jones planned the Crystal Palace around a colour-maker's ideal proportion, George Field's, of three yellow to five red to eight blue [8]. Jones got his way only in part, because the industrial paints he had to use were duller than artists' pigments, and the building ended up with a dirty off-yellow, a pale blue and a heavy brownish red [8].

The lesson is that brownish red is what an iron-based red becomes when it is cheap, thick and unrefined. The standards agree. Our library lists the name in RAL, the German paint standard, under two numbers, 3009 and 8012, and in Ridgway's 1912 plates and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 [15]. Maerz and Paul's dictionary dates the English phrase to 1847 [15].

There is also an older, unsupported idea that colours carry fixed meanings. Birren records an aura chart from occult writing that assigns a brownish red to sensuality [14]. Birren presents it as opinion, and there is no evidence that any colour triggers one fixed feeling [14].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
This is the colour of our swatch, #6E3B31, a dark brownish red [15]. Our archive of 23,781 paintings is photographed in museums, so everything below is as photographed, through aged varnish [16]. It appears in 1,099 of them, 4.62 per cent, which is more common than 84 per cent of the named colours [16].

It is a colour of the 1300s to 1500s [16]. It peaks in the 1400s, found in 50 of 945 paintings, 2.2 times the museums' baseline [16]. No painter stands out against that baseline, and the most devoted, C. W. Eckersberg, has it in 6 of 50 works [16]. Among countries, Tibet stands out, with the colour in 10 of 47 paintings, 6.1 times the expected rate [16]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent, in 50 per cent of the 577 paintings where we can rank it by lightness [16].

Within six units, the names that turn up on the same canvases most are [[mahogany]] and [[brick]] [16]. The painting with the largest share of it, nearly 60 per cent of the canvas, is a Ragamala folio from about 1750 in the Cleveland Museum [16]. The earliest match, in 1100, is a Metropolitan Museum object, and the archive's early centuries are thin, so that is a floor, not a first [16].

In printed English the phrase peaks in the early nineteenth century, close to Syme's book, and by 1980 it was used about a sixth as often as at its peak [17]. Where to look: the pigmented shadows of an Italian altarpiece, where a warm earth red has been mixed down with black, are close to the swatch [16].
